newsitem.title: FRANCE: Wheat firms lobby EU to ditch trade vow to U.S.
newsitem.headline: Wheat firms lobby EU to ditch trade vow to U.S.

text.p: The grain industry put pressure on the European Union on Thursday to brave the threat of a trade spat with the United States by abandoning a pledge on the price of wheat, grain executives said.
European traders blame an EU policy of holding down wheat export subsidies, to avoid undercutting U.S. prices, for losing them business to cheaper selling from Argentina and elsewhere.
"If this continues we are going to see our markets pinched by Argentina, Australia and Canada," veteran grain trader Jean-Pierre Dresti of French miller Soufflet said on Thursday.

Farm leaders of the United States and European Union, meeting in Rome last week, avoided stirring up past tensions over grain subsidies when the EU lowered export aid for wheat farmers. The move prevented them undercutting U.S. growers.

But on Thursday grain exporters in France, Europe's leading producer, were trying to persuade the EU's executive Commission to reverse policy by handing out subsidies large enough to take on the cheaper non-U.S. wheat directly.
Thursday is the day when grain firms have to guess the amount of grain subsidy the EU is willing to pay by sending in bids for export assistance to a weekly auction in Brussels.

The subsidies are meant to help farmers compete by bridging the gap between generally higher prices in Europe and lower prices elsewhere. But facing trade warnings over subsidies from the Clinton administration, Brussels has been reluctant to knock out U.S. wheat sales by subsidising too aggressively.

French traders said they were trying to secure subsidies for more than half a million tonnes of EU wheat on Thursday by putting in bids for subsidies between 14.4 Ecus ($18) and 24 Ecus ($30) a tonne.

Even though wheat prices have plunged from record highs earlier this year, a partial recovery in U.S. prices on Wednesday meant granting the request would put EU wheat prices below U.S. ones for the first time in months, traders said.
They calculated that with the lowest subsidy being sought by exporters, the price of French wheat would be $160 a tonne compared with $163 or $164 for similar grades in the U.S.
If the EU took the rare step of granting the highest subsidy sought, French wheat would go for under $150.
The EU was due to respond to the bids later on Thursday.
Despite record wheat prices near $300 a tonne earlier in April, the prospect of new tension over subsidies has resurfaced as prices fall under the weight of big global harvests.

A bumper crop in Argentina means that country's wheat is being sold for less than $140 a tonne. And a rebound from drought in the soon-to-be-harvested Australian wheat belt has drawn warnings of fiercer competition early next year.
U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said after the Rome talks with EU farm chief Franz Fischler last week that Brussels was honouring its pledge not to undercut U.S. farmers.
But in a sign that Washington is reluctant to give its trade rival a free rein, Glickman said he had not ruled out using U.S. subsidies to counter excessive market distortions.
Washington and the EU waged often bitter subsidy battles in the wheat market until last year, when low stocks sparked off the rise in prices and made the costly effort unnecessary.
The U.S. now says subsidies are out of date but has so far tolerated an EU decision to resume subsidising in September.
European traders want the EU Commission to ignore the risk of a subsidy confrontation with Washington, saying the U.S. cannot afford to get into a fight because its stocks remain low.
But analysts say the EU, facing budget pressures at home because of the cost of dealing with mad cow disease, is unlikely to go as far as many of the traders want.
Leading French trader Etienne Caen said in remarks published on Thursday that the EU, with a big crop this year, might lose business but had a difficult job balancing grain needs at home.
